node.label: Elizabeth Fox-Genovese
node.date_label: The Origins of Physiocracy (1976) · Within the Plantation Household (1988) · The Mind of the Master Class, with Eugene D. Genovese (2005)
node.description: Elizabeth Fox-Genovese argued that race and class shaped the lives of enslaved and slaveholding women so deeply that a shared gender did not produce a common experience. Within the Plantation Household: Black and White Women of the Old South (1988) challenges the use of models derived from New England to explain plantation households. C. Vann Woodward praised its research but disputed its treatment of Mary Chesnut’s dissent, arguing that benefiting from slavery did not automatically invalidate her criticism of it. In The Mind of the Master Class (2005), written with Eugene D. Genovese, Fox-Genovese examined the historical and religious thinking of the slaveholding elite. Steven Hahn praised its learning while questioning its claims to represent a broader ruling-class outlook and its limited analysis of gender and enslaved people’s participation.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Origins of Physiocracy: Economic Revolution and Social Order in Eighteenth-Century France (1976); “Placing Women’s History in History” (1982); Fruits of Merchant Capital: Slavery and Bourgeois Property in the Rise and Expansion of Capitalism (1983), with Eugene D. Genovese; Within the Plantation Household: Black and White Women of the Old South (1988); The Mind of the Master Class: History and Faith in the Southern Slaveholders’ Worldview (2005), with Eugene D. Genovese.
node.scope_note: Read the 1978 letter and reply, Woodward’s 1988 and Fredrickson’s 1984 reviews, selected Hahn review passages, the opening of the 1982 essay and the publisher excerpt of The Mind of the Master Class. Complete books, the remainder of the 1982 essay and the 1973 and 1976 articles remain unread. Bibliographic records establish dates only.

proposed_edges.relationship: Fox-Genovese and Eugene Genovese coauthored Fruits of Merchant Capital (1983) and The Mind of the Master Class (2005), the latter studying history and Christian faith in slaveholders’ thinking.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the Cambridge publisher excerpt, Prologue p. 1 and joint running credits, for The Mind of the Master Class. Read Hahn’s Divine Rights (2006), paragraph beginning Neither Genovese’s subsequent book, for the joint Fruits of Merchant Capital (1983). The Oxford Academic bibliographic header for Rawley’s review independently confirms both authors and 1983. Coauthorship establishes joint work, with no division of authorship or influence between the authors inferred. Retain comparison and directed false: Task M explicitly requires directed false exactly for comparison, overriding the older contribution/undirected convention cited in the finding.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Tuchman and History” (1978), Fox-Genovese challenges Stone’s professional-status test and his assumptions about progress and fourteenth-century crisis.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete letter, paragraphs beginning “It is saddening” and “Stone doubts,” web lines 85–99; A Distant Mirror (1978) unread. Criticism addresses his review.
proposed_edges.map_label: Challenges Stone on authority and crisis

proposed_edges.relationship: In his reply in “Tuchman and History” (1978), Stone rejects Fox-Genovese’s objections by distinguishing innovative research from scholarly popular synthesis.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete reply, numbered point 1, web lines 109–122; “haute vulgarisation” names his distinction. No agreement or reconciliation inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: Fox-Genovese’s “Tuchman and History” (1978) defends A Distant Mirror (1978) for connecting social groups, political choices and material dislocation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Letter’s final three paragraphs, web lines 97–99. Tuchman explicitly does not share the Marxist perspective used in her defence; her book unread. Person route specifies the speaker of existing group route edge_555.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing Within the Plantation Household (1988), Woodward disputes Fox-Genovese’s treatment of Mary Chesnut’s criticism of slavery as an anomaly, arguing that a privileged beneficiary of slavery could still criticize it with integrity.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: “Slaves and Mistresses” (1988), paragraphs beginning “As for those whose response” through “It is even possible,” web lines 140–150. “respectful exceptions” qualifies disagreement; he also praises the book. Original unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hahn’s “Divine Rights” (2006) criticizes The Mind of the Master Class (2005), jointly by Fox-Genovese and Eugene Genovese, for asserting broader hegemony without demonstrating it and underanalysing gender and enslaved participants.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read review, paragraphs beginning “Is there, finally,” “Now it may well be,” “Perhaps more striking” and “Most troubling,” web lines 63–67. “we never see this happening” targets hegemony. Also praises the scholarship. Book read only in publisher excerpt; parallel edge_2355 already targets Eugene.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hahn: hegemony, gender and absent participants

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Placing Women’s History in History” (1982), Fox-Genovese uses Du Bois’s divided consciousness to frame women’s historical inclusion.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Opening, lines 8–12: “twoness”; expressly refuses equating racial and female experience. Du Bois original unread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Placing Women’s History in History” (1982) credits Kelly’s account of feminist theory’s double perspective on social and sexual oppression.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Opening, lines 12–13: “doubled vision.” Underlying Kelly essay unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Placing Women’s History in History” (1982) credits Davis with showing how cultural forms reveal implicit gender relations and their reversals.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Opening, line 23: “taught us”; charivari specified. Davis originals unread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: Within the Plantation Household (1988) makes relations between enslaved and slaveholding women central to women’s history, arguing that race and class divide experiences that gender alone cannot explain.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher description, web lines 68–69, and Woodward’s review, lines 90–98: “class and race.” Mediated reading; book unread. Existing women roster retained.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Placing Women’s History in History” (1982) proposes analysing gender systems as historically changing relations of power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Opening, line 18, propositions 1–2: “historically, not biologically.” Remainder unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Fredrickson reads Fruits of Merchant Capital (1983), Fox-Genovese and Eugene Genovese criticize social history that separates subordinate groups from relations of political domination.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: “Class Act” (1984), web lines 121–129, especially “principal targets” and “politics of domination.” Named-reader mediation; 1983 collection and 1976 precursor unread. Shared credit retained.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Gendering Property, Racing Capital” (2014), Catherine Hall argued that Elizabeth Fox-Genovese and Eugene D. Genovese’s account of Southern paternalism and its anti-capitalist politics had little correspondence with her team’s findings about British slave-owners’ brutality and commitment to industrial capitalism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Hall’s open-access publisher text, especially the adjacent sentences naming both Genoveses and contrasting their interpretation with the British evidence. This is a challenge to the model’s applicability across settings, not a claim that Hall disproves their interpretation of the American South. Hall discusses their corpus without identifying one particular book here. Checked 2026-11-01.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hall questions the paternalism model’s applicability

proposed_edges.relationship: Fox-Genovese’s joint scholarship with Eugene D. Genovese, including Fruits of Merchant Capital (1983), helped shape Gramscian Marxist interpretations of slavery and capitalism, as Michael Kazin stated in his 1988 reply in The New York Review of Books.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the published letter and Kazin’s reply. Kazin expressly attributes an effect on many scholars to the pair’s theoretical contributions; the subsequent discussion names their 1983 collection and also criticizes idealization of slaveholders. The impact belongs to their joint body of work, not demonstrably to this book alone. The collection itself remains unread. The field endpoint denotes Marxist historical interpretation, not party membership or agreement with every British Marxist historian.
proposed_edges.map_label: Gramscian interpretations of slavery and capitalism
